title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in the EFL Writing Context: Students' Literacy in Perspective
extended_summary:
This paper examines EFL learners’ literacy in using generative AI tools for writing support, rather than testing whether AI tools improve writing outcomes through an intervention. The study asks how familiar students are with generative AI for EFL writing, whether that literacy differs by background characteristics, and what students perceive as the main challenges and affordances of such tools.

The study used a descriptive-survey design with a closed-item questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The sample consisted of 278 undergraduate EFL students from a public higher education institution in Saudi Arabia, specifically from English and translation departments. Quantitative analysis summarized students’ self-reported literacy across tasks such as brainstorming, translation, grammar and spelling help, paraphrasing, vocabulary support, and generating writing prompts, while nonparametric tests examined differences by specialization, GPA, and generative AI mastery level. Twenty students also participated in interviews to elaborate on challenges, affordances, and suggestions.

Findings showed a generally medium level of generative AI literacy overall. The highest-rated uses involved vocabulary learning, improving clarity and concision, punctuation/spelling/capitalization help, and translation. Specialization did not significantly affect responses, but GPA and mastery level did. Interview data suggested that students saw generative AI as easy to use and useful for personalized learning and feedback, while also noting problems with organization, word choice, and prompt-related skills. The paper concludes that students are positively disposed toward generative AI for EFL writing, but further training and support are needed.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools or large language model chatbots used for producing, revising, translating, and giving feedback on text and language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper surveyed EFL undergraduates’ literacy and perceived use of generative AI tools for supporting writing tasks such as translation, brainstorming, drafting, paraphrasing, grammar checking, vocabulary support, and real-time feedback.

findings.finding_summary: This descriptive survey found that EFL undergraduates reported a medium overall level of generative AI tools literacy for writing support (total mean=3.15, SD=1.134; n=278). The strongest self-reported items were help with punctuation/spelling/capitalization (mean=3.42), making writing clearer and more concise (mean=3.42), learning new vocabulary (mean=3.72), and suggesting synonyms or more sophisticated words (mean=3.41).
findings.measure: Questionnaire ratings of generative AI literacy for EFL writing tasks

findings.finding_summary: Responses did not differ significantly by specialization (Translation vs English; Mann-Whitney U, p=.120), but did differ by GPA (Kruskal-Wallis, p=.000) and mastery level of generative AI tools (Kruskal-Wallis, p=.012). Higher GPA students (4-5) had higher mean ranks than lower GPA groups, and the paper reports significant group differences by mastery level, though the direction is described inconsistently in the text.
findings.measure: Group differences in questionnaire total scores by specialization, GPA, and AI mastery level

quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a descriptive survey with interviews, not an experimental study of tool effects on outcomes. It provides correlational and self-reported evidence about literacy and perceptions, which is useful but not causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: No causal effect sizes on reading/literacy achievement are reported, and the study measures perceived literacy rather than learning gains. The practical signal is moderate self-reported readiness/usage, but direct outcome impact is unclear.
